words.intro: Ludwig II of Bavaria spent his life and all his money building castles out of the operas he loved. He lived in the most famous one for a total of 172 days.

grammar[0].fact: In the 1880s Neuschwanstein had telephones, central heating and hot and cold running water. Beneath the medieval look Ludwig insisted on the very latest technology, including an electric bell for his servants, and a lift for his food.

grammar[1].blocks[0].rows[0].en: If I had time, I would come.
grammar[1].blocks[0].rows[1].en: If he were rich, he could travel.
grammar[1].blocks[1].title: A sigh: nur, doch
grammar[1].blocks[1].text: *Wenn ich nur mehr Zeit hätte!* — If only I had more time! *Wäre ich doch zu Hause geblieben!*
grammar[1].fact: Germans have a rich word for it: *Fernweh*, the longing for far-off places, the opposite of *Heimweh*. And there’s *Torschlusspanik*, gate-closing panic: the fear that life’s chances are running out. Ludwig had both.

opener.caption: Schloss Neuschwanstein: nie fertig, und heute das berühmteste Schloss in Deutschland.
document.intro: The real ticket centre below the castle. Everyone in this photo is in the queue for a thirty-five-minute tour of a king who wanted to be alone. Read the sign over the door.
document.fact: Tickets are for a fixed minute. If you are late, the tour goes without you. The castles of Ludwig II have brought Bavaria far more money than they ever cost it, so history’s mad king turned out to be quite a good investor.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Finish each sentence in your own words.
document.tasks[1].note: Your own answers: the real verb goes at the end.
reading.intro: Lena and Maya are on a tour of Neuschwanstein, thirty-five minutes, in a group of sixty. Their guide’s name is Korbinian. He has said the same words seven times today. In the throne room, Maya whispers something that he hears.
reading.photos[0].caption: König Ludwig II. von Bayern: Er hat nie viel regiert.
reading.fact: Neuschwanstein gets about 1.4 million visitors a year, in tours of about 35 minutes. Most of its rooms were never finished. In 1886 Ludwig II was declared insane and removed from power; a few days later, he and his doctor were found dead in Lake Starnberg, in shallow water. It has never been explained.
